screens.title: Data Transformation with Aggregation Stages
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the aggregation stages that let you reshape, enrich, and persist MongoDB data. You will learn how to break arrays into individual documents with unwind, perform left outer joins using lookup, and change document structure with addFields, set, and unset. Finally, we will cover how to write pipeline results back to the database with out and merge. Each stage solves a specific transformation need: unwind makes array elements addressable; lookup brings related documents into a result; addFields and set let you compute and store derived values; unset removes fields you don’t want to expose. The out stage replaces a collection with pipeline output, while merge updates or inserts results into a target collection without destructive replacement. These tools are essential for reporting, ETL, and denormalizing data for clients. A practical example in this chapter demonstrates unwinding student enrollments, joining course records, building a grade summary, and merging counts into a summary collection. Watch for performance trade-offs: unwind can inflate document count, and lookup can be expensive without careful filtering or indexing. By the end, you should understand when to use each stage and how to combine them safely for real workloads.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Aggregation stages let you transform nested and related data inside MongoDB for reporting and ETL without exporting to external tools. Use them carefully to balance expressiveness and performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Data Transformation
Data Transformation with Aggregation Stages
Reshape arrays, enrich documents with related collections, compute fields, and persist results.

In this chapter we focus on practical composition of stages: unwind, lookup, addFields/set, unset, out, and merge. Learn when each is appropriate, common pitfalls, and performance hints that matter in production.

In this lesson
  • Deconstruct arrays so each element becomes a document with $unwind.
  • Join documents across collections using $lookup and localField/foreignField pairing.
  • Create and remove fields with $addFields, $set, and $unset; persist results with $out or $merge.
Coming up
Hands-on pipeline: unwind student enrollments, lookup course details, compute a grade string, group by course, and merge counts into a summary collection.
Explore Key Topics
$unwind — flatten arrays to operate on elements directly.
$lookup — left outer join to enrich documents from another collection.
$merge / $out — write pipeline output to collections safely.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Visual pipeline preview
Terminal demo mode
Unwind
Explodes array elements into individual documents
Lookup
Left outer join that adds matched documents as an array
Merge / Out
Persist pipeline output to a collection
Starter example
Students have enrolledCourses arrays. We'll unwind them, lookup course info, compute a combined grade string, and then group and merge counts into a summary collection.

That skill matters because many collections store related items as arrays, and you often need to analyze or group by individual elements. Second, you will learn to perform left outer joins using lookup. This allows you to enrich documents with related records without denormalizing your storage model. Third, you will manipulate document fields with addFields, set, and unset to compute derived values and remove unwanted fields. Lastly, you will understand how to persist aggregation results with out and merge, and when to choose one over the other. Each objective includes a short why-it-matters note and a mnemonic to help you remember the stage behavior. By the end of the chapter, you should be able to compose pipelines that unwind arrays, join related collections, compute and clean fields, and safely write results for reporting or incremental updates.

keyIdea.title: Practical checks
keyIdea.text: Always consider document growth from unwind, filter before lookup to reduce work, and choose merge when you need incremental updates rather than full replacement.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Objectives — Deep Dive
Unwind — practical notes
  • Unwind turns each array element into a document copy. Expect more documents downstream.
  • Use preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true to keep documents without arrays when needed.
  • Think about group and index implications when you plan to group by unwound fields.
Lookup — practical notes
  • Lookup produces an array of matches; you may unwind it if you expect a single match.
  • Filter early to reduce the number of lookups performed.
  • Indexes on the foreignField greatly improve performance.
Field transforms
  • $addFields and $set compute new values; both overwrite by default.
  • Prefer $set stylistically for newer pipelines; both are equivalent in behavior.
  • Use $unset to remove private fields before output or storage.
Out vs Merge
  • $out replaces the target collection entirely — destructive but simple.
  • $merge lets you control matching and update behavior, suitable for incremental updates.
  • Test merge options in staging to avoid unexpected replacements.

screens.title: $unwind — deconstruct array fields
screens.narratorSegment: The $unwind stage deconstructs an array field from input documents, outputting a separate document for each element. In practical terms, if a document has an items array with three elements, $unwind will yield three documents that each contain the original fields plus one of those elements. This transformation is necessary when you need to match, project, or group by properties of array elements. For example, if orders store items arrays and you want to compute total quantity per product, unwind lets you group on the productId found in each item. A common variant is preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true which keeps documents that have no array or an empty array; use it when you need to retain records that lack the array field. Watch out for a common misconception: $unwind does not remove duplicates from the array — it only expands elements. That expansion can dramatically increase pipeline work and memory use, so plan to filter early or limit arrays before unwinding. Example: an order with two items becomes two documents after {$unwind: "$items"}, each with identical order metadata but a single items sub-document. Key takeaway: use $unwind to make elements addressable, but balance document growth and pipeline performance.

keyIdea.title: Unwind summary
keyIdea.text: $unwind flattens arrays into separate documents; use preserveNullAndEmptyArrays to retain missing or empty arrays and filter early to control growth.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › $unwind
$unwind — concept and usage
Deconstruct an array field so each element becomes its own document.
Example transformation
// Original document:
// { _id: 1, orderId: "A1", items: [{productId: "P1", qty: 2}, {productId: "P2", qty: 1}] }

// After {$unwind: "$items"}:
// { _id: 1, orderId: "A1", items: {productId: "P1", qty: 2} }
// { _id: 1, orderId: "A1", items: {productId: "P2", qty: 1} }
When to use
  • Group by properties inside array items.
  • Match array elements on specific fields.
  • Normalize array contents for reporting.
Common mistake

Forgetting that unwind increases document count and can cause performance issues. If you only need the original document when an array is empty, set preserveNullAndEmptyArrays to true.

Key Takeaway

Use $unwind to make array elements addressable, but filter before or limit arrays to control pipeline size and cost.

screens.title: $lookup — enriching documents with joins
screens.narratorSegment: The $lookup stage performs a left outer join between the input collection and a foreign collection in the same database. It adds a new array field to each input document containing matched documents from the foreign collection. The core parameters are from, localField, foreignField, and as. localField identifies the field in the input documents to match, foreignField identifies the field in the foreign collection, and as is the name of the resulting array. For example, when joining orders to products you might set localField to items. productId and foreignField to _id, producing a productDetails array with matching product documents. A common workflow is to use $lookup after filtering down the input to reduce work and avoid scanning many documents. Another pattern is to $unwind the result of $lookup if you expect one match per input and prefer flattened results. Watch for a misconception: $lookup does not automatically perform a single-document replacement; it always produces an array of matches and you control whether to unwind or aggregate further. Performance is improved when the foreignField is indexed. Use lookup for ad-hoc enrichment and denormalization in read pipelines but consider pre-joining or caching if joins are frequent and expensive.

keyIdea.title: Lookup summary
keyIdea.text: $lookup performs a left outer join and returns matches in an array; filter early and ensure indexes on the foreignField to keep it efficient.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › $lookup
$lookup — parameters and pattern
Use from, localField, foreignField, and as to perform a left outer join.
Lookup example
db.orders.aggregate([
  {
    $lookup: {
      from: "products",
      localField: "items.productId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "productDetails"
    }
  }
]);
When to place $lookup
  • Prefer applying $match first to reduce input documents.
  • Use $project to include only the fields required for matching to shrink intermediary documents.
  • Index foreignField in the from collection for faster lookups.
Unwind after lookup?

If you expect at most one match per input, you can $unwind the productDetails array to simplify downstream processing. If multiple matches are expected, keep the array and aggregate accordingly.

Common Mistake

Running $lookup before filtering large collections can cause heavy resource use; always try to reduce the working set first.

screens.title: Unwind + Lookup in a student enrollments example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete pipeline using the students and courses example from the chapter. Suppose students have an enrolledCourses array of documents with courseId and grade. First we $unwind enrolledCourses so each enrollment becomes a document. That makes it simple to match and join on courseId. Next we use $lookup with from set to courses, localField to enrolledCourses. courseId, foreignField to _id, and as to courseInfo. The result is each enrollment document enriched with a courseInfo array. Often the courses collection uses string _id values that match courseId, so the lookup returns a single-element array; you can then $unwind courseInfo if you prefer a flattened shape. A key benefit of this approach is that you can compute derived fields per enrollment, like combining student name, course title, and grade into a single string, then group by course title to count enrollments. A misconception to avoid is expecting lookup to replace fields; it appends matches as an array and you must control projection to remove or reshape fields you don't need. This pipeline pattern is powerful for building reports that combine nested arrays and related collections.

keyIdea.title: Pattern
keyIdea.text: Unwind enrollments, lookup course details, optionally unwind courseInfo, then project or compute derived values for grouping and reporting.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Unwind + Lookup Example
Starter pipeline
We begin with students, unwind enrollments, then lookup courses by courseId.
db.students.aggregate([
  { $unwind: "$enrolledCourses" },
  { $lookup: {
      from: "courses",
      localField: "enrolledCourses.courseId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "courseInfo"
    }
  }
]);
Concrete outcome

Each enrollment document now contains courseInfo, an array of matching course documents. You can $unwind courseInfo for a flattened result or keep the array for multi-match scenarios.

Misconception

$lookup does not implicitly merge object fields into the root document; it adds matches as an array. Use $unwind or $replaceRoot to reshape as needed.

Key Takeaway

Combine unwind then lookup to join array elements to related collections and compute per-element metrics.

screens.title: $addFields and $set — computing derived fields
screens.narratorSegment: $addFields and $set let you compute and attach new fields to documents inside an aggregation pipeline. They are effectively equivalent: $set is a more recent alias for $addFields and is commonly used in modern pipelines. Use these stages to derive values from existing fields, for example multiplying price and quantity to produce totalPrice. Because these stages overwrite fields with the same name, be deliberate with names to avoid unintentional replacement of existing data. A practical example: after unwinding an enrollment and joining the course, you might add a studentCourseGrade field that concatenates the student name, course title, and grade into a single readable string like "Alice - Intro to MongoDB (A)". This computed field is useful for display or for downstream grouping. A common misconception is expecting addFields to be non-destructive; it can overwrite existing data. Also, computing expensive expressions repeatedly can be costly; whenever possible compute once and reuse the field later in the pipeline. Key takeaway: use addFields or set to compute clear, reusable values, and prefer explicit naming to protect your original fields. $addFields and $set — computing derived fields means $addfields and $set compute derived fields; they overwrite by default, so choose names carefully and compute once when possible.. In practical terms, create or overwrite fields based on expressions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › $addFields / $set
Compute derived values
Use expressions like $multiply and string concatenation to build useful derived fields.
Example
{$addFields: { totalPrice: { $multiply: ["$price", "$quantity"] } }}
Use case — studentCourseGrade

Compose a readable grade string combining student name, course title, and grade so reports display concise information without extra processing.

{$addFields: { studentCourseGrade: { $concat: ["$name", " - ", { $arrayElemAt: ["$courseInfo.title", 0] }, " (", "$enrolledCourses.grade", ")" ] } }}
Common Mistake

Using the same field name unintentionally with addFields or set can overwrite original values. If you need both, write to a new field name.

screens.title: $unset — remove fields before output
screens.narratorSegment: $unset removes specified fields from documents in the pipeline. It is commonly used to drop sensitive information, internal notes, or large fields that are not needed by clients or summary collections. For example, after enriching and computing fields for a report, you might unset internalNotes or a raw debug field before returning results. Unset accepts a single field name or an array of field names. A practical point: unset operates on the current document shape in the pipeline, so if you added a temporary field earlier for computation and no longer need it, unset removes it. A misconception to avoid is thinking unset returns the removed value elsewhere — it simply drops the fields. Also remember that unset does not change storage; it affects only pipeline output unless you write the results back to a collection using out or merge. Use unset to keep outputs lean and to avoid leaking internal data into reports or downstream collections. Key takeaway: unset is a simple and safe way to clean up pipeline results before presenting or persisting them. $unset — remove fields before output means $unset drops named fields from pipeline documents; use it to remove sensitive or unnecessary fields before returning or saving results.. In practical terms, strip unnecessary or sensitive fields from documents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › $unset
Remove fields confidently
Unset helps sanitize output and reduce document size before output or storage.
Example
{$unset: "internalNotes"}
When to unset
  • Before returning documents to a client.
  • Before writing to a summary collection to avoid storing large or private fields.
  • After temporary computations that created helper fields.
Key Takeaway

Unset is the clean-up step in a pipeline; use it to make outputs lean and safe for sharing or persistence.

screens.title: $out vs $merge — choose how to persist results
screens.narratorSegment: Both $out and $merge write aggregation results to collections, but they behave differently and serve different use cases. $out writes the entire pipeline result to a specified collection and replaces the collection if it exists. This is simple and predictable, but destructive: you lose previous data unless you copy it beforehand. $merge, on the other hand, gives fine-grained control. It lets you specify the target collection, the matching fields (on), and what to do when a match is found (whenMatched) or not found (whenNotMatched). Options for whenMatched include replace, merge, keepExisting, fail, or a custom pipeline. Use $merge for incremental updates, maintaining historical rows, or building materialized views where you want to update specific documents rather than overwriting everything. A frequent scenario: daily summaries where you insert new date keys and update existing summaries — here merge with on: "_id" and whenMatched: "merge" preserves prior results while updating counts. A misconception is assuming $merge cannot create a target collection; it can. Key takeaway: prefer $out for simple full replacements and $merge for controlled, idempotent updates in ETL workflows. $out vs $merge — choose how to persist results means $out replaces target collections; $merge lets you update, insert, or merge results conditionally, making it preferable for incremental or idempotent writes.. In practical terms, when to replace a collection and when to merge incrementally. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › $out vs $merge
$out — full replacement
Writes pipeline output to a collection and replaces it if it exists.
{$out: "monthly_sales_report"}
$merge — controlled updates
Merge allows matching, merging, inserting, or other behaviors when interacting with existing documents.
{$merge: {
  into: "daily_summary",
  on: "_id",
  whenMatched: "merge",
  whenNotMatched: "insert"
}}
When to prefer $merge

When you need incremental updates, materialized views, or idempotent ETL that preserves existing historical or aggregated data.

screens.narratorSegment: This lesson builds a pipeline that starts from students, explodes enrolledCourses into one document per enrollment, enriches each enrollment with course details, computes a readable grade string per enrollment, groups to count enrollments per course, and finally uses $merge to persist counts into a summary collection. Step one is $unwind: it creates a document for each enrollment. Step two is $lookup to bring course metadata into a courseInfo array. Step three uses $addFields or $set to create studentCourseGrade combining student name, course title, and grade. Step four groups by courseInfo. title and computes totalEnrollments with a $sum: 1. Step five writes the result using $merge into courseEnrollmentSummary with on: "_id" or on: course title, and whenMatched: "merge" to update counts. Be mindful that grouping by course title assumes titles are stable and unique; using a course id as _id is generally safer. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Enrollment Summary Pipeline
Full pipeline (starter)
A complete aggregation that unwinds, looks up, computes and merges results.
db.students.aggregate([
  { $unwind: "$enrolledCourses" },
  { $lookup: {
      from: "courses",
      localField: "enrolledCourses.courseId",
      foreignField: "_id",
      as: "courseInfo"
    }
  },
  { $addFields: {
      studentCourseGrade: { $concat: ["$name", " - ", { $arrayElemAt: ["$courseInfo.title", 0] }, " (", "$enrolledCourses.grade", ")"] }
    }
  },
  { $group: { _id: { title: { $arrayElemAt: ["$courseInfo.title", 0] } }, totalEnrollments: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $merge: { into: "courseEnrollmentSummary", on: "_id", whenMatched: "merge", whenNotMatched: "insert" } }
]);
Practical caution

Group keys should be stable and unique. Prefer using course id as the _id for merging rather than textual titles to avoid collisions when titles change.

Key Takeaway

Compose stages in the right order: filter, unwind, lookup, compute, group, then persist. This reduces resource usage and yields correct summaries.

screens.title: Performance considerations and common pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Transformations can be expressive, but they have operational costs. The two major performance considerations are document growth from stages like $unwind and the cost of joins with $lookup. $unwind can multiply the number of documents in the pipeline; if an array contains many elements, subsequent stages will run for each element. Plan to filter input documents early and consider truncating or slicing arrays when possible. With $lookup, the cost primarily comes from matching many input documents to an external collection. You can reduce cost by placing $match and $project stages first to shrink the working set and by ensuring the foreignField has an index in the joined collection. A common pitfall is performing a large $lookup across unfiltered inputs, which can be far more expensive than performing the same join after narrowing the set. Another pitfall is using $out on a production collection unintentionally; remember it replaces entire content. When using $merge, test whenMatched behaviors to avoid unintended merges or overwrites. Key operational advice: test pipelines on representative data, monitor memory and execution time, and prefer merge for incremental updates rather than out when historical data must be preserved. These checks help keep pipelines efficient and safe in production.

screens.title: Assessment: unique comment authors pipeline
screens.narratorSegment: A short assessment reinforces the learning. You have a posts collection where each document contains a comments array of embedded documents with author and text fields. The goal is to find all unique author names across all comments in all posts. Unwind flattens comments into individual documents; grouping by the author deduplicates them, and project outputs a clean author field.

Projection alone cannot deduplicate; grouping or set-based operators are required to get unique values.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the aggregation stages that let you reshape, enrich, and persist MongoDB data. You will learn how to break arrays into individual documents with unwind, perform left outer joins using lookup, and change document structure with addFields, set, and unset. Finally, we will cover how to write pipeline results back to the database with out and merge. Each stage solves a specific transformation need: unwind makes array elements addressable; lookup brings related documents into a result; addFields and set let you compute and store derived values; unset removes fields you don’t want to expose. The out stage replaces a collection with pipeline output, while merge updates or inserts results into a target collection without destructive replacement. These tools are essential for reporting, ETL, and denormalizing data for clients. A practical example in this chapter demonstrates unwinding student enrollments, joining course records, building a grade summary, and merging counts into a summary collection. Watch for performance trade-offs: unwind can inflate document count, and lookup can be expensive without careful filtering or indexing. By the end, you should understand when to use each stage and how to combine them safely for real workloads.

These objectives set clear, practical outcomes you will achieve. First, you will be able to deconstruct array fields into separate documents using the unwind stage. That skill matters because many collections store related items as arrays, and you often need to analyze or group by individual elements. Second, you will learn to perform left outer joins using lookup. This allows you to enrich documents with related records without denormalizing your storage model. Third, you will manipulate document fields with addFields, set, and unset to compute derived values and remove unwanted fields. Lastly, you will understand how to persist aggregation results with out and merge, and when to choose one over the other. Each objective includes a short why-it-matters note and a mnemonic to help you remember the stage behavior. By the end of the chapter, you should be able to compose pipelines that unwind arrays, join related collections, compute and clean fields, and safely write results for reporting or incremental updates.

Now we expand each objective with practical checks and common pitfalls. For unwind, be ready for increased document count; always consider preserveNullAndEmptyArrays when missing arrays matter. For lookup, aim to place a match early in the pipeline and ensure foreign keys are indexed to reduce work. For addFields, set, and unset, remember that addFields and set can overwrite existing fields — choose names carefully and avoid accidental data loss. Unset is useful for removing internal notes or secrets before returning results. For out and merge, the difference is critical: out replaces the entire target collection, which is simple but destructive, while merge offers conditional updates or inserts and is better for incremental ETL. A key practical check is to run expensive stages after filtering when possible, and always test merge strategies in a staging environment to avoid unexpected overwrites. These expansions help you move from knowing a stage exists to using it safely in pipelines that run in production.

The $unwind stage deconstructs an array field from input documents, outputting a separate document for each element. In practical terms, if a document has an items array with three elements, $unwind will yield three documents that each contain the original fields plus one of those elements. This transformation is necessary when you need to match, project, or group by properties of array elements. For example, if orders store items arrays and you want to compute total quantity per product, unwind lets you group on the productId found in each item. A common variant is preserveNullAndEmptyArrays: true which keeps documents that have no array or an empty array; use it when you need to retain records that lack the array field. Watch out for a common misconception: $unwind does not remove duplicates from the array — it only expands elements. That expansion can dramatically increase pipeline work and memory use, so plan to filter early or limit arrays before unwinding. Example: an order with two items becomes two documents after {$unwind: "$items"}, each with identical order metadata but a single items sub-document. Key takeaway: use $unwind to make elements addressable, but balance document growth and pipeline performance.

The $lookup stage performs a left outer join between the input collection and a foreign collection in the same database. It adds a new array field to each input document containing matched documents from the foreign collection. The core parameters are from, localField, foreignField, and as. localField identifies the field in the input documents to match, foreignField identifies the field in the foreign collection, and as is the name of the resulting array. For example, when joining orders to products you might set localField to items. productId and foreignField to _id, producing a productDetails array with matching product documents. A common workflow is to use $lookup after filtering down the input to reduce work and avoid scanning many documents. Another pattern is to $unwind the result of $lookup if you expect one match per input and prefer flattened results. Watch for a misconception: $lookup does not automatically perform a single-document replacement; it always produces an array of matches and you control whether to unwind or aggregate further. Performance is improved when the foreignField is indexed. Use lookup for ad-hoc enrichment and denormalization in read pipelines but consider pre-joining or caching if joins are frequent and expensive.

Let's walk through a concrete pipeline using the students and courses example from the chapter. Suppose students have an enrolledCourses array of documents with courseId and grade. First we $unwind enrolledCourses so each enrollment becomes a document. That makes it simple to match and join on courseId. Next we use $lookup with from set to courses, localField to enrolledCourses. courseId, foreignField to _id, and as to courseInfo. The result is each enrollment document enriched with a courseInfo array. Often the courses collection uses string _id values that match courseId, so the lookup returns a single-element array; you can then $unwind courseInfo if you prefer a flattened shape. A key benefit of this approach is that you can compute derived fields per enrollment, like combining student name, course title, and grade into a single string, then group by course title to count enrollments. A misconception to avoid is expecting lookup to replace fields; it appends matches as an array and you must control projection to remove or reshape fields you don't need. This pipeline pattern is powerful for building reports that combine nested arrays and related collections.

$addFields and $set let you compute and attach new fields to documents inside an aggregation pipeline. They are effectively equivalent: $set is a more recent alias for $addFields and is commonly used in modern pipelines. Use these stages to derive values from existing fields, for example multiplying price and quantity to produce totalPrice. Because these stages overwrite fields with the same name, be deliberate with names to avoid unintentional replacement of existing data. A practical example: after unwinding an enrollment and joining the course, you might add a studentCourseGrade field that concatenates the student name, course title, and grade into a single readable string like "Alice - Intro to MongoDB (A)". This computed field is useful for display or for downstream grouping. A common misconception is expecting addFields to be non-destructive; it can overwrite existing data. Also, computing expensive expressions repeatedly can be costly; whenever possible compute once and reuse the field later in the pipeline. Key takeaway: use addFields or set to compute clear, reusable values, and prefer explicit naming to protect your original fields. $addFields and $set — computing derived fields means $addfields and $set compute derived fields; they overwrite by default, so choose names carefully and compute once when possible.. In practical terms, create or overwrite fields based on expressions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

$unset removes specified fields from documents in the pipeline. It is commonly used to drop sensitive information, internal notes, or large fields that are not needed by clients or summary collections. For example, after enriching and computing fields for a report, you might unset internalNotes or a raw debug field before returning results. Unset accepts a single field name or an array of field names. A practical point: unset operates on the current document shape in the pipeline, so if you added a temporary field earlier for computation and no longer need it, unset removes it. A misconception to avoid is thinking unset returns the removed value elsewhere — it simply drops the fields. Also remember that unset does not change storage; it affects only pipeline output unless you write the results back to a collection using out or merge. Use unset to keep outputs lean and to avoid leaking internal data into reports or downstream collections. Both $out and $merge write aggregation results to collections, but they behave differently and serve different use cases. $out writes the entire pipeline result to a specified collection and replaces the collection if it exists. This is simple and predictable, but destructive: you lose previous data unless you copy it beforehand. $merge, on the other hand, gives fine-grained control. It lets you specify the target collection, the matching fields (on), and what to do when a match is found (whenMatched) or not found (whenNotMatched). Options for whenMatched include replace, merge, keepExisting, fail, or a custom pipeline. Use $merge for incremental updates, maintaining historical rows, or building materialized views where you want to update specific documents rather than overwriting everything. A frequent scenario: daily summaries where you insert new date keys and update existing summaries — here merge with on: "_id" and whenMatched: "merge" preserves prior results while updating counts. A misconception is assuming $merge cannot create a target collection; it can. This lesson builds a pipeline that starts from students, explodes enrolledCourses into one document per enrollment, enriches each enrollment with course details, computes a readable grade string per enrollment, groups to count enrollments per course, and finally uses $merge to persist counts into a summary collection. Transformations can be expressive, but they have operational costs. The two major performance considerations are document growth from stages like $unwind and the cost of joins with $lookup. $unwind can multiply the number of documents in the pipeline; if an array contains many elements, subsequent stages will run for each element. Plan to filter input documents early and consider truncating or slicing arrays when possible. With $lookup, the cost primarily comes from matching many input documents to an external collection. You can reduce cost by placing $match and $project stages first to shrink the working set and by ensuring the foreignField has an index in the joined collection. A common pitfall is performing a large $lookup across unfiltered inputs, which can be far more expensive than performing the same join after narrowing the set. Another pitfall is using $out on a production collection unintentionally; remember it replaces entire content. When using $merge, test whenMatched behaviors to avoid unintended merges or overwrites. Key operational advice: test pipelines on representative data, monitor memory and execution time, and prefer merge for incremental updates rather than out when historical data must be preserved. These checks help keep pipelines efficient and safe in production.

These three concise concept cards summarize what you should remember. First, $unwind deconstructs arrays into multiple documents and is essential when you need to operate on individual elements, but it can increase pipeline size. Second, $lookup performs left outer joins and appends an array of matches; always reduce the input set and index the foreignField for performance. Third, $merge and $out persist results: out overwrites the target collection, while merge allows controlled updates and inserts, making it suitable for incremental ETL and materialized views.
